contract_plain_english: A real random variable X is sub-gaussian exactly when its square X² is sub-exponential, and the norms satisfy the exact identity ∥X²∥ψ1 = (∥X∥ψ2)².

source_evidence.observation: The lemma states: a random variable X is sub-gaussian if and only if X² is sub-exponential; moreover, ∥X²∥ψ1 = ∥X∥ψ2².
The proof identifies ∥X²∥ψ1 with the infimum of K > 0 satisfying E exp(X²/K) ≤ 2 and ∥X∥ψ2 with the infimum of L > 0 satisfying E exp(X²/L²) ≤ 2, saying the definitions become the same with K = L².

source_evidence.location: PDF page 16; printed page 27; and PDF page 22; printed page 33
source_evidence.observation: The source definitions are ∥X∥ψ2 = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2} and ∥Z∥ψ1 = inf {t > 0 : E exp(|Z|/t) ≤ 2}; for Z = X², |Z| = X².

conclusions: X is sub-gaussian if and only if X² is sub-exponential.
definitions_and_conventions: For the nonnegative random variable Z = X², |Z| = X².
implicit_context: Sub-gaussian and sub-exponential class membership is understood through the equivalent properties in Propositions 2.5.2 and 2.7.1 and the two definitions.
All expectations are taken with respect to the ambient probability law of X.

details: The class-membership result is a biconditional, not merely a one-way implication.
The ψ1 norm of X² equals the square of the ψ2 norm of X with exact constant 1.
No centering, independence, boundedness, or nondegeneracy assumption is stated.
The proof is a direct change of scale K = L² between the two exponential-moment norm definitions.

undebatable_constraints: The sub-gaussian/sub-exponential membership statement is an if-and-only-if.
The transformed variable is exactly X².
The norm conclusion is the exact equality ∥X²∥ψ1 = ∥X∥ψ2², not an inequality up to an absolute constant.
No independence or mean-zero assumption may be added.
